paper_title: From Retrieval to Typed Decisions: Calibrated System One Models from Biomedical Sentence Encoders

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Typed decision models answer schema-constrained questions about a text in one forward pass and return probabilities meant to be thresholded. We ask whether biomedical sentence encoders trained for retrieval are good starting points for such models. We present SBERT2S1, which converts Sentence-Transformers encoders into bi-encoder, cross-head (C) and prior-fused residual (PFR) decision models, together with BIODECIDE, a biomedical typed-decision suite, and MEDLINE-S1, 243k training decisions derived from NLM indexing. Across six parent-retriever pairs, retrieval training improves zero-shot matching of content-bearing options. After fine-tuning, its effect depends on the head: across five pairs and three training-set sizes, retrieval training significantly helps PFR, which keeps the retrieval prior, in 10 of 15 comparisons, but helps C in one and hurts it in five. A matched grid of two heads and five training objectives shows that C outperforms PFR under every objective, and that the released RLCD recipe of open System One models trails cross-entropy by 2.5-3.0 points. The deficit stems mainly from its reward normalisation, which inflates the noisy score-function term 3.6-15-fold; an unbiased leave-one-out estimator recovers most of the gap. After temperature scaling, no objective is clearly better calibrated than cross-entropy. We release the code, the MEDLINE-S1 labels and a model.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Much of the language processing in biomedical software consists of small, bounded decisions: does this abstract report randomised trial, does the evidence support the claim, how severe are the side effects patient describes? Because the answers are consumed by code, decision is only useful if it respects schema and comes with confidence that can be thresholded to act, defer or escalate. 1 Request State: title and abstract of PubMed citation choice: Study design? {RCT, cohort, case report, . . . } noul: Did the study involve human participants? score: Strength of evidence? System One request pairs state with typed questions. biomedical sentence encoder, converted with one of four heads (3), returns calibrated distribution over each questions options in one forward pass, and downstream code thresholds it to act or escalate. Example values are illustrative. System One models were proposed for exactly this interface (TypeSafe AI, 2026). request pairs text (the state) with typed questions of three kinds (choice, score and noul), and the model returns, in one forward pass, distribution over the options each question allows. The open model Laya (Convai Innovations, 2026) pairs an encoder with mask-slot head and trains it with RLCD, mixture of cross-entropy and policy gradient against proper scoring rules (Gneiting and Raftery, 2007). All existing System One models are generaldomain and start from masked-language-model (MLM) or decoder checkpoints. Most biomedical encoders are MLMs too, such as BioBERT (Lee et al., 2020) and PubMedBERT (Gu et al., 2021). smaller group has been further trained contrastively as Sentence-Transformers encoders for retrieval: S-PubMedBERT-MS-MARCO (Deka et al., 2022) is PubMedBERT fine-tuned on MS MARCO (Nguyen et al., 2016), and MedCPT (Jin et al., 2023) is trained on PubMed search logs. typed decision resembles retrieval, since it asks whether hypothesis formed from question and an option matches the state, but retrieval similarity need not encode negation, ordinal judgement or calibrated truth. This study tests whether biomedical sentence encoders can be converted into System One models, and what the result depends on: RQ1 Initialisation: when does retrieval training improve zero-shot or fine-tuned decisions? RQ2 Conversion: how do bi-encoder, cross-head and prior-fused conversions trade accuracy, robustness to option order, cost and retrieval retention, under matched objectives? RQ3 Objective: which ingredient of RLCD matters once temperatures are fitted: the proper score, the noise smoothing, or the policygradient estimator? Contributions. (1) SBERT2S1, framework that turns Sentence-Transformers encoders into typed decision models with four conversions, including prior-fused residual (PFR) head that starts from the calibrated zero-shot retriever; (2) BIODECIDE, biomedical typed-decision suite with public and credentialed clinical tracks, and MEDLINE-S1, multi-question training data labelled from NLM indexing rather than an LLM teacher; (3) controlled study over eleven encoders, six parentretriever pairs, and matched grid of two heads and five objectives; and (4) an analysis showing that RLCD optimises noise-smoothed proper score, that the released estimator is biased and rescaled, and that simple leave-one-out baseline removes both problems. sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: System One models. Jev (TypeSafe AI, 2026) introduced typed decisions with three primitives: choice (one option from schema), score (a distribution over an ordinal rubric) and noul (the probability that statement holds); its training objective is not public. Laya (Convai Innovations, 2026), the first open implementation, pairs ModernBERTlarge (Warner et al., 2025) with two-layer head that scores one [MASK] slot per option, trained with cross-entropy plus group-baselined policy gradient (as in GRPO; Shao et al., 2024) on noiseperturbed logits rewarded by proper scores. De2 cider (Marosi, 2026) fine-tunes decoders, and the Decision Index (Decision Index contributors, 2026) benchmarks typed-decision engines. Concurrent work applies or probes System One models in security agents, annotation, crash-report coding, distracting contexts and active questioning (dos Santos, 2026; Ibrahim and Zaki, 2026; Rafe and Das, 2026; Xu, 2026; Yilmaz et al., 2026) (Appendix A). These studies do not evaluate biomedical conversions, retrieval initialisation, or RLCD ablations. Calibration and scoring rules. strictly proper scoring rule is uniquely optimised in expectation by the true distribution (Gneiting and Raftery, 2007); examples include the log, Brier (Brier, 1950), spherical and ranked-probability (Epstein, 1969) scores. Neural networks, including pre-trained transformers, are often miscalibrated, and temperature scaling is strong post-hoc remedy (Guo et al., 2017; Desai and Durrett, 2020). calibration benefit claimed for training objective must therefore survive temperature scaling. Sentence encoders as decision models. Siamese encoders trained so that cosine similarity reflects relatedness (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019), on query-passage data such as MS MARCO (Nguyen et al., 2016), are standard for dense retrieval; cross-encoders re-rank more accurately at higher cost (Nogueira and Cho, 2019). Comparing text with label descriptions underlies entailmentbased zero-shot classification (Yin et al., 2019). In biomedicine, domain pre-training (Gu et al., 2021) followed by contrastive training on search logs (Jin et al., 2023) or MS MARCO (Deka et al., 2022) yields strong retrievers. We use such encoders as the initialisation of decision models and measure what the contrastive stage adds.

sections.content: Temperatures. After training, one temperature per type and option-count bucket (K = 2, 35, 610, 11) is fitted by minimising negative loglikelihood on calibration split carved from the training data before training, with per-type fallback for buckets with fewer than ten items. Every metric is reported before and after this step. Long states. Clinical notes exceed the 512-token context of base encoders. Besides truncation and sliding windows, we evaluate retrieve-then-decide: the models own embedding eθ selects the = 3 note chunks most similar to the instruction x, and the decision is made on those chunks in document order. This requires the converted model to remain retriever.

sections.title: 6.1 RQ1: Does retrieval training help?
sections.content: Retrieval improves zero-shot content matching. Without training, every contrastive checkpoint reaches 1524 chance-normalised points on questions whose options differ in content (disease areas, study designs, specialties, rubrics, exam answers), against 07 for their MLM parents and 20.3 for Laya-large  (Table 3)  . On options that differ only by label word (yes/no, true/false), cosine gaps are of order 103 and no encoder is reliably above chance. After fine-tuning, retrieval benefits depend on the head. With full data and the cross head the contrastive stage is roughly neutral: S-PubMedBERT and PubMedBERT reach 67.7 and 67.3, both MPNet checkpoints 66.4, and the BioClinicalModernBERT pair 72.9 and 73.1  (Table 2)  ; the only Holm-significant difference is negative (GTEModernBERT 2.5; Table 8). With PFR, which keeps the retrieval prior, the retriever is better in three of five pairs (all-MPNet +4.5, Nomic +2.7, GTE +2.9), worse for S-PubMedBERT (1.6), and the ModernBERT embedders gain +10.9 on held-out tasks (Holm .014 for each). With less data the heads diverge further (Figure 2). For PFR, retrievers are ahead in four of five pairs at both 10% and 2% (significant in three and four; e.g. Nomic +5.3 and +9.2, GTE +4.7 and +7.4, and up to +16.3 on held-out tasks). For C, the ModernBERTfamily retrievers are 2.53.7 points behind their parents at 10%, BioClinical-ModernBERTs embedder is 8.5 points behind at 2%, and the only gain is S-PubMedBERT at 10% (+1.9). MedCPTQuery illustrates the dependence on the conversion: its [MASK] states are identical within an input, so the cross head reaches only 17.9, but PFR reaches 60.4. The strongest base-size model is BioClinicalModernBERT with cross head (73.1), close to fine-tuned Laya-large (75.0) at about third of its size. sections.title: 6.2 RQ2: Which conversion works best?
sections.content: The cross head achieves higher accuracy. In the matched grid  (Table 4)  , exceeds PFR by 1.3 2.4 seen-task points for all five shared objectives (Holm .011 for CE, Proper and PG; .08 and .14 for PG-LOO and Reparam) and by 3.810.2 points on held-out tasks. The bi-encoder matches on seen tasks (0.6, n.s.) but loses 9.4 held-out points; its value is that state embeddings can be precomputed for corpus screening. frozen prior improves PFR by 2.5 points. Prior fusion reduces option-order sensitivity. Prior fusion makes decisions almost invariant to option order: averaged over all evaluation splits, random permutation changes 0.3% of SPubMedBERT PFR answers versus 15.7% for C, whose flips concentrate on unseen inputs (held-out 17%, exams 28%, seen tasks 3%; Appendix H). sections.title: 6.4 LLMs and confidence-based routing
sections.content: Fine-tuned encoders are competitive on seen tasks: S-PubMedBERT trained with CE (70.2) and Laya-large (75.0) exceed zero-shot Gemma-4-31B (65.7) and Qwen3.8-27B (57.4), with better calibration (ECE after scaling 3.84.3 vs. 8.59.1). The LLMs achieve higher accuracy on held-out tasks (Gemma 52.6 vs. 31.0), the clinical track (81.683.4 vs. at most 38.4 zero-shot, 55.2 with clinical training) and exams. The two are complementary (Figure 3): routing the 20% least confident questions to Gemma raises macro accuracy over seen and held-out tasks from 59.5 to 68.4 for SPubMedBERT (CE) and from 64.3 to 69.1 for Laya-large, against 62.1 for Gemma alone. This is retrospective fixed budget on the test set, not validated deployment threshold.

sections.title: 7 Discussion
sections.content: Retrieval benefits depend on the head. Retrieval training helps zero-shot and helps priorfused head, more so with scarce labels, but is close to neutral for cross head with full data and can cost accuracy with few labels. Lines: mean over three encoder seeds; bands: sd. tion is therefore most beneficial when the conversion retains the retrieval prior (PFR), particularly with scarce labels; it offers no consistent accuracy gain for cross head. Choosing conversion. For per-request decisions, we recommend cross head with crossentropy (70.2 on S-PubMedBERT). BioClinicalModernBERT with cross head reaches 73.1 under PG. PFR is preferable when low option-order sensitivity is important or when the encoders mask-slot states are degenerate, and when corpus must be screened against many questions. Every trained conversion degrades the embedding as retriever unless the prior is frozen.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: Biomedical sentence encoders trained for retrieval can be converted into System One models: with cross head they reach 6673 seen-task points with top-label ECE below 6 after temperature scaling (MedCPT-Query excepted), close to finetuned Laya-large (75.0) at about third of its size. Whether retrieval training itself helps depends on the conversion: it helps PFR in 10 of 15 comparisons, most clearly with little labelled data, but does not consistently help C. Plain cross-entropy with temperature scaling matches or outperforms the released RLCD recipe, whose deficit comes from its reward normalisation; implementations of RLCD should use an independent baseline such as leave-one-out. Fast encoders and LLMs are complementary, so calibrated System One model is natural first stage that answers confident cases and escalates the rest.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Scope. Results cover base-size encoders, one fixed training budget and hyperparameters inherited from Laya; objectives were not tuned separately, and the head objective grid was run on one encoder. The six parent-retriever comparisons share parents and differ in retrieval corpora, so they are not independent replications. Intervals condition on the observed tasks and seed-averaged correctness; no mixed-effects or equivalence analysis is claimed. Data. MEDLINE-S1 labels are weak: indexing can omit tags and uses the full article. few exact training inputs recur in calibration and test splits; we report the (small) sensitivity of test scores but did not retrain or refit temperatures on de-duplicated splits. Text-level identity cannot establish patient-level independence or exclude nearduplicates. Exam contamination of the LLMs is unmeasured. Calibration and shift. Low ECE on seen tasks does not imply calibration on new tasks: on heldout tasks several models are poorly calibrated, and option-order sensitivity of cross heads grows under shift. Thresholds should be validated on in-domain samples before use. Clinical use. The clinical tests are small, come from one hospital system and use surrogate names; long-note strategies remain close to chance for base encoders. Nothing here is validated clinical device, and the released model is not trained on clinical notes.

sections.title: Ethics Statement
sections.content: Credentialed PhysioNet data (MedNLI, MIMICIII and MIMIC-IV derivatives) were used under their data use agreements, processed only on institutional infrastructure, and never sent to hosted model or API; only aggregate metrics leave that infrastructure, and examples in this paper are paraphrased. Public datasets are used under their published licences or terms of use; for them we release conversion code and per-record hashes rather than the data. For MEDLINE-S1 we release PMIDs, questions and labels under CC BY 4.0 without the abstracts, which script retrieves from PubMed. The released model is trained only on public data and inherits the non-commercial licence of S-PubMedBERT-MS-MARCO. Calibrated confidences can encourage automation; we recommend human review of escalated and low-confidence decisions in any health-related deployment.

sections.content: The probe (Table 6, Figure 5) holds the model, batch and noise level fixed and compares estimators of the gradient of the smoothed score with respect to the logits. Three results are consistent across PFR checkpoint trained with PG, one trained with PG-LOO, and checkpoint trained with CE. Second, the released normalisation multiplies the estimate by 3.63.8 at σ = 0.4 and by 1415 at σ = 0.1, so relative to cross-entropy the score term weighs 4.75.0 and then 1920 times as much, against 1.3 for the unbiased estimators. Figure 6 shows the consequence during training: every objective is clipped at every step, and under PG the clipped direction is dominated by the inflated, noisy score term. sections.title: L Released Software and Model
sections.content: The code release contains the four conversions, the five objectives (including PG-LOO), temperature fitting, the long-state strategies, the data builders, script that restores the MEDLINE-S1 abstracts from PubMed, and the evaluation and bootstrap code used here. The released model is the best seed (by seen-task accuracy) of SPubMedBERT-MS-MARCO with cross head trained with CE on public data (seen 70.5; threeseed mean 70.2 0.4). Inference is single file of plain PyTorch (sbert2s1.py) that ships with the model.
